nameStory: Choreocolax polysiphoniae doesn't have a common name because it's such a tiny, specialized organism that most people never encounter it. The scientific name Choreocolax comes from Greek words meaning 'dancing' and 'parasite,' which hints at its unique lifestyle of living on other seaweeds. It's named after its host species, polysiphoniae, which refers to the red algae it parasitizes.
description: This is an extremely tiny parasitic red alga that lives on other seaweeds along New England's rocky shores. You'd need a magnifying glass or microscope to really see it properly, as it appears as minute bumps or growths on its host algae. It's not a typical plant but rather a marine alga that has evolved to steal nutrients from other red seaweeds. Think of it as nature's tiniest seaweed vampire.

idTips.label: Size and visibility
idTips.description: Extremely small - appears as tiny bumps or nodules that you'll need magnification to identify properly

idTips.label: Host relationship
idTips.description: Always found growing on other red algae, never free-living on rocks or surfaces

idTips.label: Color
idTips.description: Usually appears as small reddish or pinkish growths that may be slightly different in color from the host seaweed

idTips.label: Texture
idTips.description: Feels like tiny firm bumps when you run your finger over the infected seaweed

habitat: Found in the intertidal and subtidal zones along New England's rocky coastlines, always attached to other red algae. Look for it on exposed rocky shores and tide pools where its host seaweeds grow abundantly. It's most likely to be found in areas with good water circulation and wave action.

seasonality.spring: May begin appearing on host algae as water temperatures rise and seaweed growth accelerates.
seasonality.summer: Peak growing season when it's most visible on its host seaweeds during low tide explorations.
seasonality.fall: Still present but may be harder to spot as host algae begin their seasonal changes.
seasonality.winter: Persists in milder winter conditions but growth slows significantly in cold water.

funFact: This tiny parasite is so specialized that it can only survive by hijacking the cellular machinery of specific red algae species - it's essentially a seaweed that gave up photosynthesis to become a microscopic pirate!
confusionNotes: Could be confused with other small growths on seaweeds like barnacles, bryozoans, or reproductive structures of the host algae. Unlike these, Choreocolax feels soft and squishy rather than hard, and it's always reddish in color rather than white or gray.
contextualKnowledge: This represents one of nature's most specialized parasitic relationships - it's so adapted to its parasitic lifestyle that it can't survive without its host. Most beachcombers walk right past millions of these tiny organisms without ever knowing they exist.
compareHints: Since this is the only Choreocolax species in New England waters, compare it to other small parasitic red algae in the same family. Unlike free-living red algae that attach to rocks, this species only grows on living seaweed hosts. Other parasitic algae may form different shapes or target different host species.
